On entend beaucoup parler de « pénurie d: We hear a lot about “labour shortages” and “temporary immigration,” but very little about what people who come to Quebec to work actually go through. For some, the dream turns into a nightmare. That is the case for Patrick, Fouad and other former employees of the Iris agency, whom I met at a rally held in front of the company to denounce its practices.
J’ai parlé longuement avec Fouad et Patr: I spoke at length with Fouad and Patrick, as well as with people from the Centre des travailleurs et travailleuses immigrants (CTTI), who have been supporting them through their legal and administrative steps for months.
J’ai évidemment tenté de communiquer ave: Of course, I tried many times to reach the Iris agency and its director, Dieudonné Nidufasha. I went to his office and sent him an email, as well as messages on LinkedIn and Facebook, all in vain. I also contacted the Commission des normes, de l'équité, de la santé et de la sécurité du travail (CNESST) to get its perspective, without success.
<strong>Ils sont venus pour travailler,: They came to work, to provide for their families, to build a better life in a country known for its social justice. This Monday morning, under a grey spring sky in LaSalle, about a dozen of them gathered in front of the former offices of the Iris agency, holding signs that spelled out their rage: “Sick of being treated with contempt!”
« Cette entreprise a voulu nous esclavag: “This company wanted to enslave us,” says Patrick*, a former employee of the Iris placement agency in LaSalle. Like him, several former workers came to denounce an injustice that turned their lives upside down: that of a closed immigration and work permit system that, instead of protecting them, exposed them to abuse. Yet the use of closed work permits by placement agencies is a practice prohibited in Quebec. Such a work permit is normally tied not only to a single employer, but also to a single position. However, to “rent out” these immigrants’ labour to third-party companies anyway, some placement agencies look for legal loopholes. That is the case of the Iris agency.
Des visages fatigués, mais déterminés. D: Tired but determined faces. Anonymously or openly, these immigrants tell the same stories. Unpaid hours, contracts never received, pay stubs nowhere to be found and, above all, the constant fear of being deported because of the irregular status they were pushed into.
« Près de 20 d’entre eux ont déposé une: “Nearly 20 of them have filed a complaint with the Commission des normes, de l'équité, de la santé et de la sécurité du travail (CNESST) – more than a year ago for some,” explains Laura Doyle Péan, a member of the Centre des travailleurs et travailleuses immigrants (CTTI). The Montréal organization has supported their fight for many months. Banner, signs and flyers – the watchword of this morning’s rally at the foot of the building housing the placement agency’s offices is simple: keep up the pressure.
« Pendant un an, alors qu’il y avait de: “For a year, even with numerous complaints, nothing happened, and the agency was able to continue its practices without being bothered,” says Manuel Salamanca Cardona, a community organizer with the CTTI.
Ce n’est qu’après la médiatisation de l’: It was only after the case was covered by Le Devoir four weeks ago that things started to move, he notes. “All of a sudden, after Labour Minister Jean Boulet spoke in the article, the CNESST decided to pull the Iris agency’s permits.”
En effet, depuis le 1<sup>er </sup>janvi: Indeed, since January 1<sup>st</sup>, 2020, recruitment and placement agencies must obtain a permit issued by the CNESST. Since that permit was suspended, the company run by Dieudonné Nidufasha can no longer operate legally. The CNESST is also pursuing legal action for unpaid wages totalling nearly $100,000. It is a first victory for these vulnerable workers, but it is far from enough, as their future remains uncertain.

Toujours selon <em>Le Devoir</em>, M. Ni: According to Le Devoir, Mr. Nidufasha allegedly obtained closed permits for about fifty immigrants among the 180 employees his placement agency recruited during its operations. This foreign workforce reportedly worked for 18 companies in Montréal, Laval, the Laurentians and other regions.
Les conséquences de cette affaire vont b: The consequences of this affair go well beyond money. The psychological stress caused by administrative instability, by the inability to pay rent or feed one’s family, and by the fear of deportation has left deep marks. Some workers report sleep disorders and chronic anxiety… Patrick and Fouad, two of the victims of this scheme, agreed to share their stories with us.
<strong>« Il savait qu’on n’avait person: “He knew we had no one to turn to, and he took advantage of it”
« Je venais juste pour un mois, pour vis: “I was only coming for a month, to visit. But I really liked Quebec, and my friends told me there were work opportunities here,” says Patrick. Convinced, he decided to look for a job. That is when an acquaintance told him about Dieudonné Nidufasha and his agency. What he didn’t know then was that this decision would lead him into what he considers a spiral of abuse and exploitation. “We suspected nothing. The manager seemed nice, jovial, professional, and we would have trusted him with our lives. We thought he really wanted to help us,” says Patrick. The reality turned out to be completely different for the man who arrived in June 2023 from his native Cameroon.
Il finit par obtenir le permis de travai: He ended up getting the work permit promised by the agency, after four months of waiting and paying $1,250 in cash to the director – a completely illegal practice. “The conditions of the Temporary Foreign Worker Program (TFWP) and the International Mobility Program (IMP) prohibit employers from charging recruitment fees to workers and hold them responsible for recruiters’ actions in this regard,” confirms Immigration, Refugees and Citizenship Canada (IRCC).
Pire encore, Patrick affirme ne pas avoi: Worse still, Patrick says he received no temp assignment for several months. The agency had nevertheless promised him enough contracts to amount to full-time work. And when he was finally offered work, it was not what he expected. “He called me and just said: ‘Are you ready for an adventure in northern Quebec?’” says the man in his fifties.
Il découvre que le poste est situé à Riv: He discovered that the position was in Rivière-du-Loup, more than 400 km from Montréal, in a seniors’ residence. “My work permit was valid for the production machine operator category, but I ended up – without any training – as an attendant for seniors,” he continues. He had no choice but to accept. Indeed, with a so-called closed work permit, Patrick was tied to his employer: the Iris agency.
À Rivière-du-Loup, l’adaptation est diff: In Rivière-du-Loup, adjusting was hard. “The first month was fine. The second, a bit less… Then Dieudonné started doing whatever he wanted. He paid us twice a month, sometimes only once, even though the residence paid a salary every week. I was paid half my wages several times,” Patrick says.
Il évoque un système opaque : des jours: He describes an opaque system: unpaid workdays, incomprehensible deductions and, above all, total confusion about his rights. “He knew we couldn’t say no. He knew we had no one to turn to, and he took advantage of it.”
<strong>Comment signaler des abus aux au: How can abuse be reported to the authorities?
Les travailleurs étrangers temporaires v: Temporary foreign workers who are victims of mistreatment or violence can report it through Service Canada’s confidential tip line, either by filing a report with an agent or by leaving a message. To do so, call 1-866-602-9448. An <l1>online reporting tool</l1> is also available.
« C’est le moyen le plus efficace pour l: “This is the most effective way for the government to identify and deal with bad actors. The government’s <l1>confidential line</l1> is available 24 hours a day, 7 days a week, and agents provide services in 200 languages,” says IRCC. By phone or online, no personal information is required, and the government never tells the employer or anyone within the company the identity of the person who made a report.
Enfin, n’importe qui peut effectuer un s: Finally, anyone can make a report, even if they are not the person affected. A co-worker, an ordinary citizen or an organization aware of abuse or violence against temporary foreign workers can take action.
Au fil des mois, Patrick sombre dans la: Over the months, Patrick sank into precarity, and the situation became harmful to his mental and physical health. He developed a severe stomach ulcer that landed him in the hospital. “The doctor said it was because of stress,” he says. Fearful, he at first refused to confide in the health professional, before giving in to the doctor’s insistence. “I told him about my working conditions, and he explained that it wasn’t normal, that it was illegal and that I should file a complaint with the CNESST.”
Lorsqu’il finit par se tourner vers la C: By the time he finally turned to the CNESST, it was too late for him to benefit from the protective measures available to vulnerable workers. His work permit having expired in October 2024, he lost his legal status. “I wanted to file a complaint earlier, but the head of the residence talked me out of it. He said it would create problems. I thought I was being loyal, but I’m the one who ended up without status,” Patrick says.
Aujourd’hui hébergé par sa sœur à Laval,: Now staying with his sister in Laval, he is fighting to regularize his situation. But without documents, without formal proof of employment, he is hitting a wall. “I just want what I went through to be recognized. They took advantage of me because I was vulnerable. I did everything I could to be honest. And I was let down.” Today, the Iris agency still owes him $2,500 in back pay.
Sans statut, Patrick n’est pas autorisé: Without status, Patrick is not allowed to work and can no longer provide for his wife and son, who remained in Cameroon while waiting for him to bring them over. It is a reality that is hard for the father to bear. “I explained the situation to my wife, but she thinks I’m lying and that I’ve started a new life here with another woman. It’s very hard for me, because unfortunately, some African men have done that, but I don’t want to abandon my family.”
Honteux de ne pouvoir soutenir les siens: Ashamed of being unable to support his loved ones and feeling guilty about depending on his sister to survive, he knows the months ahead will be long and painful. But he remains determined to fight for his rights and regain his dignity. In the meantime, he can count on the solidarity that has formed among the agency’s former workers.
<strong>« J’ai pris une journée de congé: “I took a day off so I could be here today and make my voice heard”
« Je suis arrivé le 28 juillet 2023 », s: “I arrived on July 28, 2023,” recalls Fouad, who is originally from Algeria. The young man thought he could quickly enter the job market thanks to his experience in the oil sector. A year later, his drawn features suggest instead a path strewn with obstacles, vague promises and Kafkaesque procedures. “Even though it didn’t suit my employer, I took a day off so I could be here today and make my voice heard.”
Le ton est calme, posé, mais la lassitud: His tone is calm and measured, but weariness can be sensed behind his words, spoken sometimes in French, sometimes in Arabic. When he arrived in Canada on a tourist visa, Fouad hoped to turn his stay into a professional opportunity. “A friend told me about the agency. He said people had gotten work permits in a few weeks,” he says. So he contacted Dieudonné Nidufasha, who invited him to an information meeting.
« On était un groupe d’une quinzaine de: “There were about fifteen of us, and he explained all the steps we had to take. He told us we had to pay him $1,250 cash to get a work permit, and that once we had it, he would give us assignments to work full time,” says the man in his thirties. Fouad thought he was dealing with a professional looking for labour for sectors facing worker shortages. He suspected nothing.
Le jeune homme suit les étapes conseillé: The young man followed the steps recommended by the agency: paying $1,250 in cash to the agency’s director, booking a hospital appointment for the medical exam, then submitting his file to Immigration, Refugees and Citizenship Canada (IRCC). After four long months of waiting, during which Fouad lived off his savings, his work permit was finally approved.
Mais alors qu’il s’attend à avoir des of: But while he expected to receive assignment offers from the placement agency, nothing came. “They told me they would look for a job for me, but that it would be good if I found interested employers myself and told them to go through the agency to hire me. I was very surprised!” Fouad says.

Il ajoute n’avoir eu aucune proposition: He adds that he had no offers for another four months. “It was very hard, I had no money left,” the young man confesses, lowering his gaze. Trapped in an extremely precarious situation, without family, he survived on the food assistance he received from some community organizations. When he was finally called to work for five months at a company, he thought things would get better.
La désillusion va être d’autant plus gra: The disillusionment would be all the greater. “After two days of work, the client told me he would call me back when he needed me,” he says. In shock, he explains that he thought it was a multi-month assignment, but learned that this had never been the plan. “Once again, I was lied to! And the worst part is, I wasn’t even paid for that work.”
À ce moment, sa situation devient critiq: At that point, his situation became critical. Fouad contacted several people, looked for solutions and eventually obtained a collective letter of support thanks to the Centre des travailleurs et travailleuses immigrants (CTTI). He is grateful for their help: “Thanks to them, I was able to get the open work permit for vulnerable workers.”
Aujourd’hui, Fouad, qui n’a jamais rien: Today, Fouad, who never told his parents about his difficulties – out of shame and modesty – wants to believe in a better future. He laments, however, that the immigration system does not protect him. “My open work permit is valid for only one year and is not renewable. It’s very hard to find an employer who agrees to a contract for just a few months,” he points out.
Grâce à son sérieux et à l’aide de la co: Thanks to his diligence and the community’s help, he has nevertheless found a full-time job paying $17 an hour. The problem is that even if this unexpected employer wanted to keep him and apply for a work permit, he wouldn’t be able to. Low-wage work permits are indeed frozen following the <l1>government measures</l1> taken at the end of last year to reduce immigration.
« Je comprends qu’ils veulent baisser l’: “I understand that they want to lower immigration, but for those who are already here and who have suffered like us, I think they should change the system and give us at least a chance,” he says without much conviction.
Lorsque nous le laissons, il discute ave: As we leave him, he is discussing with Manuel Salamanca Cardona possible solutions so that he can keep his status. “We want to keep up the pressure and stay visible on this issue. The more agency workers speak out, the better our chance of getting an answer and fixing their situation. It’s also an opportunity to revive the debate on closed work permits, which we’ve been denouncing for years, because each time the cases are different, but the human consequences are the same,” says the community organizer.
À la fin de la rencontre, une femme se j: At the end of the meeting, a woman joins us. She too is a victim of the agency: “I’m sorry, but I’ve cried too much, I can’t tell my story anymore.” The woman in her forties is unable to tell her story, so raw is the trauma. Fouad, for his part, who didn’t think his personal situation could be the subject of a CNESST complaint, is now considering filing one. One more.
Contactés à plusieurs reprises, l’agence: Contacted several times, the Iris agency and its director, Dieudonné Nidufasha, did not respond to our interview requests. On site, no one seemed to be present in the company’s offices. La Converse also requested an interview with the CNESST, without success to date.
Le débat sur le permis fermé n’est pas n: The debate over closed permits is not new. For several years, many actors, both nationally and internationally, have denounced the structural imbalance that this type of permit creates between employers and workers. In 2023, the <l1>UN Special Rapporteur</l1> on contemporary forms of slavery recommended that Canada abolish it, stressing its potential to foster human exploitation and seeing in it a form of “contemporary slavery.” Several parliamentary reports, federal and provincial, have echoed these recommendations, yet no concrete measures have been implemented.
L’affaire Iris met toutefois en lumière: The Iris affair, however, highlights the particular problem of recruitment and placement agencies. The business model is simple: recruit workers on closed permits, then “rent them out” to third-party companies, often in sectors with severe labour shortages, such as seniors’ care and construction. This practice, although prohibited under provincial law, persists under cover of regulatory complexity and lack of oversight. Some agencies, like Iris, reportedly get around the legislation by relying on legal loopholes made possible by international free trade agreements, which allow certain deviations in the placement of foreign labour.
Deux entreprises clientes de l’agence Ir: Two companies that were clients of the Iris agency, including the Résidence Reine-Antier in Rivière-du-Loup, told Le Devoir they acted in good faith. They maintain that they paid the agency all sums owed and that they were unaware of its internal practices. Yet Quebec law is clear: companies that benefit from the services of a worker recruited by a placement agency are jointly and severally liable for any breach relating to the worker’s conditions of employment. This provision is precisely intended to prevent responsibility from being diluted among several parties and to guarantee a minimum level of protection for employees.
L’histoire de l’agence Iris n’est pas un: The Iris agency’s story is not an isolated case. Other files are already emerging, driven by the same dynamics of precarity, silence and exploitation.
